title: The Voyager Missions
text: NASA launched Voyager 1 in September 1977, just weeks after its twin Voyager 2. The twin spacecraft were designed to tour the outer planets and then escape the solar system. Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter in March 1979 and Saturn in November 1980. Its discoveries include active volcanoes on the moon Io and a complex ring system around Saturn. Engineers expected the missions to last only five years, yet the probes kept returning data for decades. Both spacecraft carry a golden record with sounds and images of Earth, a message aimed at anyone who might find them. In August 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. Mission controllers still hear from Voyager 1 every day, though a signal now takes more than 22 hours to arrive. The spacecraft run on radioisotope generators whose power output falls a little every year.

title: How Coffee Is Grown
text: Coffee begins as a seed inside a bright red fruit called a cherry. Farmers grow the plants in a band of highlands near the equator, usually between the tropics. The best beans come from plants that grow at high altitude, where cool nights slow the cherries down. After picking, the fruit is either washed clean or dried whole in the sun, two methods that give the cup very different flavours. Roasters then heat the green beans until they crack, developing the aromas that drinkers recognise. A single tree can produce roughly one kilogram of roasted coffee each year. Experts such as Dr. Alvarez recommend drinking the beans within a month of roasting. Countries like Brazil, Vietnam, and Colombia dominate world production between them. Millions of smallholder families depend on the crop for their income, so price swings are felt far beyond cafes.

title: The Birth of the World Wide Web
text: Tim Berners-Lee, a physicist at CERN, proposed the World Wide Web in a memo in 1989. The memo described a system of hypertext documents linked across a network. In 1991 the first website went live for the wider internet community. Early pages were plain text, e.g. directories of research papers maintained by hand. Berners-Lee insisted that the web stay free of patents and royalties. That decision let the technology spread to every university and company almost overnight. Browsers such as Mosaic later added images and colour, which brought ordinary people online. Search engines then became essential, because finding a page was harder than publishing one. Today the web carries news, video, commerce, and government services for billions of people every day.
